pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 5-7 (KS1/Grades K-2): minibeasts in simple food chains — who eats whom (leaf → caterpillar → bird), that minibeasts are both eaters and eaten, and that the arrow means 'is eaten by' / energy flows this way.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' — describe how animals obtain their food from plants and other animals, using the idea of a simple food chain, and identify and name different sources of food. Working-scientifically: identifying and classifying.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports K-LS1-1 (what animals need to survive/food) and 2-LS4-1 (diversity of life); food-web depth comes later (5-LS2-1).
• Operational details — start with a plant as the food source (producer, though the word isn't needed yet). The ARROW is the load-bearing convention: it points from the food to the eater (leaf → caterpillar means the caterpillar eats the leaf). Minibeasts sit in the middle — a caterpillar eats leaves AND is eaten by a bird. Keep chains short (3-4 links) and real (garden creatures).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): says what one minibeast eats and one thing that eats it. Tier B (age 6): builds a correct 3-link chain and reads the arrows aloud. Tier C (age 7): explains the arrow direction ('the arrow shows who eats who — it points to the eater') and places a minibeast as both eater and eaten.
bestPractices: Teach the arrow convention explicitly and repeatedly — it points from food to feeder and shows energy passing along; misreading it is the classic error.
Always start the chain with a plant/leaf as the food source so children see where the energy enters.
Highlight minibeasts as MIDDLE links — both eater and eaten — to break the idea that a creature is only ever predator or only ever prey.
Use real, local garden chains children can picture (leaf → caterpillar → blue tit) rather than abstract examples.
Keep chains short (3-4 links) at this age; food WEBS and producer/consumer vocabulary come later.
keyRepresentations: A left-to-right food-chain diagram with clear directional arrows (leaf → caterpillar → bird).
Drag-to-order organism cards that snap into a chain.
A 'both arrows' highlight on the middle creature showing it is eaten AND eats.
Read-aloud sentence frames ('the caterpillar is eaten by the bird').
commonMisconceptions: Arrow-direction reversal — children read 'bird → caterpillar' as 'the bird is eaten by the caterpillar'; the arrow points to the eater.
'A creature is either a hunter or food' — not grasping that a minibeast can be both (eats plants, eaten by birds).
'Chains start with an animal' — missing that the plant is the starting food source.
'Big animals always eat small ones / the last animal is the strongest' — size and 'winner' confusions.
Treating the chain as who-is-friends-with-whom rather than who-eats-whom.

learn.summary: Teaches 5-7 year olds simple garden food chains: who eats whom (leaf → caterpillar → bird), that minibeasts are both eaters and eaten, and that the arrow means 'is eaten by' / energy flows toward the eater. Core activity is constructing a short chain and reading the arrows aloud; a quiz and a tap-to-reveal scene are companions; role-play is an alternative for surfacing the middle-of-chain idea. The eater is identified by its role in the chain, not by being the bigger animal.

activities.title: Build and read a garden food chain
feedback: If a child tries to link the leaf directly to the blue tit (leaf → blue tit, with no caterpillar between): ask 'in our chain, who eats the leaf?' and prompt them to find the caterpillar, which the blue tit then eats.
When the order is correct, confirm the arrow snaps into place and energy passes along leaf → caterpillar → bird.
When the caterpillar is tapped, highlight both sides so the child sees it is eaten AND eats.
If the chain is read with the arrow backwards, re-read it as 'is eaten by / energy flows to' and point to the animal that gets the meal, whatever its size.
activities.rationale: A food chain is an ordered relationship, and this activity proposes building it as a way to make who-eats-whom and arrow direction concrete rather than only viewing a finished diagram. Live feedback on wrong versus right order and an explicit 'both sides' highlight are intended to surface the reasoning. Live recolouring, snapping arrows and an energy pulse are optional interaction examples that may make the mechanism visible, not required features.
sourceClaims: The food-chain arrow convention (points from food to feeder, showing energy flow) is a known source of confusion best taught explicitly.
learnerActions: Start with a shuffled set of garden organism cards — leaf, caterpillar, blue tit — and arrange them into the correct order to show who eats what.
Place the caterpillar next to the leaf and draw or confirm an arrow from leaf to caterpillar (leaf → caterpillar).
Add the bird after the caterpillar and draw the arrow caterpillar → bird.
Tap or point to the caterpillar in the middle and say both things about it: 'I eat the leaf' AND 'the bird eats me'.
Read the finished chain aloud using the arrow convention: 'the leaf is eaten by the caterpillar, the caterpillar is eaten by the bird'.

Try the deliberate wrong move of linking the leaf directly to the blue tit (leaf → blue tit, skipping the caterpillar) to see why it does not fit this chain: in this chain the caterpillar eats the leaf and the blue tit eats the caterpillar.
Optionally remove one link and say what happens to the chain.
activities.intendedInsight: The arrow points from the food to the eater (it means 'is eaten by' and shows energy passing along), and a minibeast in the middle is both an eater and something that is eaten.

activities.title: Order, match and choose the arrow direction (companion checks)
feedback: For arrow-direction choices, confirm the arrow points toward the eater (caterpillar → bird means the bird eats the caterpillar).
For a reversed answer, re-read the arrow as 'is eaten by' and point to the animal that gets the meal, whatever its size.
activities.rationale: Ordering, matching and a direction question check the idea directly and cheaply. These are recognition-style checks: they assess and reinforce but do not by themselves require the child to construct and explain the chain, so they work best after the build-and-read activity.
sourceClaims: The food-chain arrow convention (points from food to feeder, showing energy flow) is a known source of confusion best taught explicitly.
learnerActions: Put the three organism cards (leaf, caterpillar, bird) in the correct sequence.
Match each eater to its food (bird ↔ caterpillar, caterpillar ↔ leaf).
Choose which way the arrow points between the caterpillar and the bird, and say what it means.
activities.intendedInsight: Who-eats-whom order and arrow direction can be stated reliably and transferred to a new chain.

activities.title: Interview a caterpillar (role-play alternative)
feedback: If the child says the caterpillar is only food, prompt them to name what the caterpillar itself eats.

If the child says big animals always eat small ones, offer a real counterexample: a small caterpillar eats a much bigger leaf, and a garden spider can catch an insect bigger than itself. (The ladybird is bigger than the aphids it eats, so it shows a tiny hunter, not a smaller eater.)
activities.rationale: Spoken role-play surfaces the eater-and-eaten relationship through responsive questioning and gives a distinct experience from card-building. It is offered as an alternative route into the same idea, not a replacement for constructing and reading a chain.
learnerActions: Pretend to be a caterpillar and answer two questions aloud: 'What do I eat?' and 'Who eats me?'
Say the sentence 'I eat the leaf and the bird eats me' to capture the middle-of-chain idea.
Swap roles and interview a ladybird to find out it hunts aphids.
activities.intendedInsight: A minibeast sits in the middle of a chain — it both eats and is eaten — and even a tiny creature can be a hunter.

activities.title: Read the arrow in a labelled garden scene (scaffold)
feedback: Confirm that the arrow always points to the animal that gets the meal, whatever its size.
Prompt the child to then build the same chain themselves so they move from recognising to constructing.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal scene can show a chain and name the arrow convention, which supports children who are not yet ready to build from scratch. Because the chain is already ordered for them, it functions as a scaffold; the intended deeper engagement is proposed to come from constructing and reasoning about order, so following it with the build-and-read task is recommended.
learnerActions: Look at a garden picture with a pre-drawn chain leaf → caterpillar → bird.
Tap or lift the 'what does the arrow mean?' label and read the explanation aloud.
Point along the chain in the direction the energy travels.
activities.intendedInsight: The arrow between two organisms means 'is eaten by' and shows energy moving to the eater.

constraints: Start every chain with a plant/leaf as the food source so children see where the energy enters, even though the word 'producer' is not needed yet.
Teach the arrow convention explicitly and repeatedly: it points from food to feeder and shows energy passing along; misreading it is the classic error.
Keep chains short (3-4 links) and use real, local garden creatures children can picture; food webs and producer/consumer vocabulary come later.
Highlight minibeasts as middle links — both eater and eaten — to break the idea that a creature is only ever a predator or only ever prey.
Identify the eater by its role in the chain, never by being the bigger animal; the eater can be smaller than or the same size as its food.

Ordering, matching and multiple-choice checks are recognition-style: they confirm and reinforce but do not require the child to independently construct or explain a chain. Use them after construction.
The tap-to-reveal garden scene is a scaffold with the chain pre-ordered; it supports but does not substitute for the child building and reading a chain.

Correct the size misconception directly: the eater is not always the bigger one. For example, a small caterpillar eats a much bigger leaf, and a garden spider can catch an insect bigger than itself in its web. A ladybird hunting aphids shows that a tiny minibeast can be a hunter, but it is not a size counterexample, because ladybirds are bigger than aphids.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all sources[].verified flags were false in the row and have not been re-checked. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original labelled the 3D-interactive option 'poor' with the claim '3D adds nothing'. This has been dropped as an unsupported universal claim rather than migrated as a pedagogical law; a food chain is an ordered relationship, so a spatial 3D scene is simply a weaker fit here, not inherently without value.
The original framed the tap-to-reveal scene as something a 'static reveal can't provide' learning for. Softened to a scaffold-with-a-stated-limit rather than asserting it cannot teach.

Efficacy wording was softened in the build and scaffold rationales: the claim that constructing a chain is 'best' or produces 'deeper learning' than viewing one is a plausible design rationale but is not source-verified, so it is stated as proposed/intended.
'Energy flows this way' is used at a child-appropriate level; at ages 5-7 this is an intuitive gloss on the arrow convention rather than a formal energy-transfer concept.

Candidate feedback originally directed children to 'point to the bigger animal that gets the meal' and mislabelled the deliberate wrong move as placing the leaf before the bird; both were corrected because they reinforced the size misconception and contradicted the correct leaf → caterpillar → bird ordering.

probeDeeper: The bird eats the caterpillar — so which way should the arrow point?
Name something the caterpillar eats AND something that eats the caterpillar.
Can a tiny ladybird be a hunter? What does it hunt?
assess.correctAnswer: The arrow points from the caterpillar TO the bird, meaning the caterpillar is eaten BY the bird (the food and energy pass to the bird). And yes — the caterpillar itself eats leaves. Minibeasts both eat (plants or smaller creatures) and are eaten by bigger animals.

errorPatterns.pattern: The arrow points to what the animal eats — so 'caterpillar → bird' means the caterpillar eats the bird.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-read the arrow as 'is eaten by' / 'energy flows to' — it points toward the animal that gets the meal.
errorPatterns.distractor: The arrow means the caterpillar eats the bird.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reverses the arrow, making the smaller animal the eater of the bigger.

errorPatterns.pattern: Minibeasts only get eaten — they don't eat anything themselves.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the caterpillar eating leaves — minibeasts are both eaters and eaten, links in the chain.
errorPatterns.distractor: Caterpillars are just food for birds; they don't eat anything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the caterpillar purely as food, never as a feeder.

errorPatterns.pattern: Big animals always eat small ones, so a tiny minibeast could never be a hunter.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give a counterexample — a ladybird hunting aphids — to break the size rule.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies a small creature (e.g. a ladybird) can prey on anything.

responseLevels.gap: Reads the arrow backwards or thinks minibeasts only ever get eaten.
responseLevels.full: Reads the arrow as 'eaten by / energy to,' places a minibeast as both eater and eaten, and transfers the idea to a new food chain.
responseLevels.partial: Gets who-eats-whom right but treats the chain as a one-way list, not grasping that the arrow shows energy flowing to the eater or that a minibeast both eats and is eaten.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In the food chain leaf → caterpillar → bird, what does the arrow between the caterpillar and the bird mean — who eats whom? And does the caterpillar eat anything itself?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who reads the arrow backwards says the caterpillar eats the bird. A child who understands reads the arrow as 'is eaten by / energy goes to,' and knows a minibeast both eats and is eaten.
